statements.text: The Prime Minister said the UK assesses that the incident at RAF Fairford is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran and almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard, and that the UK will not tolerate such threats on its soil. He said the UK will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks and bring further sanctions to restrict Iran and the IRGC. He said the UK has been in close contact with the US on protective security at shared bases, thanked police and military personnel for their response to the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth, and said the Home Secretary will update the House on Fairford.

The Prime Minister said the government has decided to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling support, and that a Voyager has already completed 14 operational missions. He condemned the appalling attacks on King Khalid International Airport and said the UK will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.

A UK government spokesperson said the UK will continue working with international partners to ensure Ukraine has the military and financial support it needs to defend itself, will maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, and that Russia could end the war today.

A UK government spokesperson said Ukraine has repeatedly shown it is serious about peace while Russia has repeatedly rejected full and partial ceasefires. The Prime Minister said that in the three weeks since his New York meeting with President Zelenskyy, Russian strikes have intensified, including attacks on apartment blocks and on buses carrying children. The Chancellor said Russia continues its bombardment of Kyiv and energy infrastructure.

A UK government spokesperson said the UK remains committed to supporting Ukraine for as long as it takes and to working with partners to bring about a durable peace. Andy Burnham said that rock-solid support for Ukraine is vital for keeping the UK safe and that the UK is with Ukraine for as long as it takes, and will go further and faster in its support.

The Prime Minister said an energy ceasefire, with both sides stopping their attacks, is the quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets without rewarding the aggressor, and that Ukraine wants one. He welcomed President Trump's announcement of a reciprocal energy ceasefire, and said President Zelenskyy has assured him Ukraine would implement it immediately once a start date is confirmed.

The Prime Minister said that in recent days the government announced new funding to help Ukraine get through its fifth winter under Russian bombardment, and a new sanctions package so that over 90% of Russia's oil producing capacity is now covered by UK sanctions.

The Prime Minister is set to tell President Zelenskyy that he has asked Ministers to draw up further sanctions, military support and fiscal packages to provide urgent support in the coming weeks, and will accelerate delivery of critical air defence missiles.

The UK is delivering £45 million of surface-to-air missiles to Ukraine and is standing by plans to fully implement a maritime services ban on Russian LNG. The UK will accelerate deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles, which have proven effective against jet-powered drones; it has already committed £1.6 billion to deliver more than 5,000 of them over four years, and will accelerate £10 million of the £45 million package for Ukraine's most urgent winter requirements.

speakers: Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey
statements.text: The Chancellor will urge partners at the IMF meetings in Bangkok to fully implement an equivalent ban on Russian LNG, following the UK's lead, and the Foreign Secretary did the same with partners at the Warsaw Security Forum. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey said: I urge partners to back the ban on Russian LNG, like we have done in the UK, to curtail the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants.

At Downing Street on 14 October the leaders said Russia had no interest in peace. The Prime Minister set out the UK's latest package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles in response to Russian jet-powered drone attacks, and the leaders discussed how the UK could accelerate defensive support to Ukraine ahead of the winter, including on long range missiles.

The Prime Minister said the UK would continue to develop innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners, and would continue its diplomatic efforts to support international supplies of defensive equipment.

The Prime Minister said NATO is a defensive alliance, that the UK will meet its NATO commitments in full, and that Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe. He said that in Berlin he and Chancellor Merz agreed a new partnership to tackle these hybrid threats, and confirmed a commitment to establish a new National Centre for Information Defence.

The Prime Minister said he raised the Falkland Islands and the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British with President Trump, and that the UK will always do whatever it takes to uphold the islanders' will.

The Prime Minister said the UK will take up the G20 presidency in 2027 and place AI centre stage, and that he confirmed this in New York. He said the President of Microsoft is saying Britain is the world leader in AI safety, and that the UK aims to agree a single set of global principles and standards on AI during its presidency year.

The Prime Minister told the Commons that he took a message to the UN that after a decade of turbulence Britain is back and can be relied upon as a consistent and stable partner, upholding the shared values in the UN Charter.

The Prime Minister confirmed the UK-EU summit will take place in Brussels on 20 November, and said it offers an opportunity to make progress on boosting UK growth and controlling illegal immigration. On the table are a food and drink trade deal, a deal on emissions trading and progress towards linking energy systems, a youth experience scheme, and deeper cooperation on immigration.

The Prime Minister said a food and drink trade deal is expected to add the equivalent of over £10 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040. He said the agreement on the table would lift a burden that can reach £1,400 on a single shipment for farmers and food producers, and would mean no more export health certificates, which can cost up to £200 each time, for small businesses.
The Prime Minister said the proposed energy deal with the EU could help lower energy costs for households and businesses, and could cut wholesale energy costs in Northern Ireland by 20%.

The Prime Minister told the Commons he believes the UK's chances of a summit deal are enhanced by being open to discussing its relationship with the EU in the longer term. His immediate priority is a successful outcome at the summit, and he believes a serious dialogue about the options for the long-term relationship should then be set up.

Andy Burnham said that in his first week in office he told the First Minister he wanted to work with him to spread opportunities across Scotland's regions and cities, that through No10 North the UK is rewiring the state and wants Scottish regions fully part of this, and that he is making an offer to the Scottish Government.

Douglas Alexander said devolution has done a great deal but power was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament, and that people in North Lanarkshire, Fife or the Highlands know what their communities need better than any minister. He said the Prime Minister's offer to the Scottish Government is a genuine one and the Scotland Office is ready to help make it happen.

The Prime Minister will invite Scotland's First Minister to work with him on pushing more power out of Westminster and Holyrood, and will call on the Scottish Government to work with the UK Government through No10 North and the Scotland Office to develop a new model of regional empowerment for Scotland.

The Prime Minister said he wants to make a serious and genuine offer to the Scottish Government, and in the immediate months ahead to design together a new model of regional economic empowerment across Scotland, with control in the hands of local people. He said he wants to work with the First Minister to deliver it.
The Prime Minister made an offer to Scotland of DWP devolution, a model of localised employment support similar to the one in England but shaped by Holyrood.

The Prime Minister said the National Economic Council will meet in a couple of weeks with the First Ministers of Scotland and Wales and the First Minister and Deputy First Minister of Northern Ireland, for the first time since he became Prime Minister, to put the offer on the table and work out a plan together.

The Prime Minister said the review led by Alan Milburn is challenging government to look at youth support very differently, building a system on the Easterhouse principle of names not numbers, built from the bottom up.

The Prime Minister said Scotland, the most devolved nation in the UK, is one of the most centralised nations in Europe, and that devolution was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament. He argued the next stage should place more decision-making in the hands of Scotland's regions and cities to drive reindustrialisation.
The Prime Minister said around one in six young people in Scotland are not in education, employment or training, and that he will not have a country where kids in their 20s are just on benefits.

The Prime Minister said that as Mayor of Greater Manchester he put buses back under public control and chose buses built by Alexander Dennis in Falkirk, and that he wants all public procurement in the UK to back a plan to reindustrialise Britain.
The Prime Minister said the Scottish Government has agreed to match the UK Government's £10 million to create two defence technical excellence colleges, one in the east and one in the west.
The Prime Minister said the Scottish Government has announced a long-term programme for local government reform, and that he thinks the UK must move faster and do more on regional powers.

The site of Great British Railways headquarters has been unveiled at Becketwell in Derby, a brownfield site in the city centre. The decision is described as a milestone in the plan for a publicly owned railway. Construction is expected to begin in early 2027 and be completed by spring 2029. The HQ will accommodate up to 450 GBR staff and is estimated to bring hundreds of rail jobs and a £151 million boost to Derby.
Up to 600 apprentices aged 16 to 21 will enrol over the next four years on the rail foundation apprenticeship, with the first starters based in Derby.

Andy Burnham said that for too long people have put up with a railway that often lets them down, that the Derby HQ will bring investment and good jobs and give young people the chance to build their future there, and that putting essentials back in public hands is bringing back hope.

Heidi Alexander said the biggest shake-up to the railways in a generation is underway, that Great British Railways will bring the railway together around better services for passengers with Derby at the heart of its future, and that she is delighted Becketwell will become GBR's new home.

Pat McFadden said the government is determined to build a strong pipeline of skilled workers for the rail sector, and that the foundation apprenticeship is part of a £2.5 billion youth employment support package creating up to 500,000 opportunities for young people to earn or learn.
Claire Ward said the GBR announcement is fantastic news for Derby, bringing hundreds of jobs, and that she is particularly pleased about the 600 apprenticeship places.

The King has appointed Mr William James Baxter QPM DL as Lord-Lieutenant of County Tyrone, succeeding Sir Robert William Lowry Scott, who retired on 17 June 2026. Mr Baxter served in the RUC/PSNI from 1973 to 2003, and was District Commander in Omagh in 1998, including on the day of the Omagh bombing.
